passage: Note from the class teacher. At pick-up today, Avni's drawing was torn and she was crying. Jomon said, "She took my crayon first." Their father answered, "You are older, you should know better." Jomon went quiet, folded his arms, kicked at the gravel and would not look up. On the walk to the gate he muttered, "It's not fair." I asked their father if we could hear from both children together before deciding. He agreed, crouched down, and let Jomon speak first. Jomon's shoulders slowly dropped. I will check in with both children tomorrow.

qa.q: What did their father say to Jomon at pick-up?
qa.a: Their father said, "You are older, you should know better."

qa.q: What does Jomon's behaviour after that suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Jomon felt the blame was unfair and was sulking. Folding his arms, kicking gravel, and muttering "It's not fair" all point to that.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped, and what could the father try next time?
qa.a: The teacher asked that both children be heard before deciding. Next time the father could ask each child what happened before saying who is at fault.

qa.q: How might Avni see the moment when her father lets Jomon speak first?
qa.a: Avni may see that her brother is also being listened to, and that her father wants to know what really happened. She may feel less alone in her tears too.

grounding: A parent blames the older child with "you are older, you should know better", the child feels it is unfair and sulks, and a wiser adult hears both children.

passage:
"Mummy, Trisha scribbled on my notebook!"
"And you pushed her. Reena, you are older, you should know better."
"But she did it first!"
"You're older. Say sorry."
Reena stomped into her room and hid under the blanket. "Nobody listens to me," she muttered.
That night, Papa knocked. "I heard there was a fight. Tell me what happened. Then I'll ask Trisha too."
Reena peeped out. "She scribbled on my homework page. Then I pushed."
"Pushing isn't okay. And scribbling isn't either. You'll both say sorry tomorrow."
Reena came out from the blanket.

qa.a: She scribbled on Reena's notebook, on her homework page.

qa.q: Why did Reena hide under the blanket?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair and hurt that only she was blamed, so she sulked and felt that nobody listened to her.

qa.q: What did Papa do differently from Mummy?
qa.a: He heard both children before deciding, and named what each one did wrong.

qa.q: How might Trisha see being blamed along with Reena?
qa.a: She may feel a bit caught, but it teaches her that scribbling on her sister's work matters too.

grounding: An older child is blamed just for being older and sulks at the unfairness; the other parent hears both sides before deciding.

passage:
From Kishore's notebook, after tonight's fight between my two sons.
Thomas and his little brother were fighting over the tablet. I heard a crash and shouted, "Thomas, you are older, you should know better!" Thomas went red, threw himself on his bed and would not look at me. At dinner he pushed his rice around. Later I asked both boys to tell me, one at a time. The little one admitted he grabbed the tablet and dropped it. Thomas had only shouted. I told Thomas I was sorry. Next time I will ask before I decide.

qa.q: What were Thomas and his little brother fighting over?
qa.a: They were fighting over the tablet.

qa.q: How was Thomas feeling when he threw himself on the bed?
qa.a: He felt blamed unfairly and resentful, so he sulked and would not look at Kishore.

qa.q: What will Kishore do differently next time?
qa.a: Kishore will ask both boys what happened before deciding who is to blame.

qa.q: What is it like for the little brother when both boys are asked to tell their side?
qa.a: He may feel a little guilty for letting Thomas take the blame, but also relieved to own up about the dropped tablet.

grounding: An adult blames the older boy for being older, sees him sulk, then hears both children and apologises.
